name: Sun Ra
role: American musician, composer and cosmological writer (1914–1993)
summary: Sun Ra’s public thought combines criticism of conventional democracy and militarism with spiritual transformation and cosmic social possibilities. His historical and futuristic visions cross racial boundaries, but his interviews offer few concrete positions on ordinary public policy.

sources.title: Sun Ra: Our 1989 Interview, originally SPIN April 1989
sources.author: Sun Ra, interviewed by John Farris
sources.usedFor: His comments on democracy, superior leaders, spiritual welfare and warfare.

sources.title: Interview with Sun Ra (1988), San Francisco, transcribed and edited by Dan Plonsey
sources.author: Sun Ra, interviewed by Jennifer Rycenga; preserved on Brian Zimmerman’s Sun Ra archive
sources.usedFor: Extended own-word discussion of world authority, ancient Egypt and extraterrestrial futures; distinguished from other page contents.

sources.title: Performing the Past to Claim the Future: Sun Ra and the Afro-Future Underground, 1954–1968, African American Review 45 (2012), pp. 197–203
sources.author: Daniel Kreiss
sources.usedFor: Archival reconstruction of his pan-racial social vision and synthesis of historical culture with technology.

sources.title: Sun Ra: Do the Impossible (2026), documentary and full transcript
sources.author: Christine Turner; PBS American Masters
sources.usedFor: Conscientious objection, imprisonment, Chicago activism and later career; archival speech separated from commentary.

notes: This is a limited political record despite extensive artistic and philosophical material. The review covers draft resistance in 1942–1943, Chicago pamphleteering, later lectures and recordings, and extended 1988–1989 interviews. Cosmic claims are reported as his ideas, not factual descriptions; proposals without clear institutional meaning receive low confidence. Band discipline is not treated as support for national dictatorship, and personal sexual practices do not supply family or marriage policy. Film characters, commentators and musical aesthetics do not automatically state his views. His Civil War comments distinguish the purpose of emancipation from economic causes involving slavery, so they do not establish that slavery was unimportant. Nor does describing racial exclusion by itself establish every specific corrective policy. His use of equations includes esoteric wordplay and does not establish a conventional rationalist doctrine. All statement themes and remaining nulls were reviewed. No historical inference was added.
